speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on examining Bill S-29 one is struck by one obvious value that shines through it. I refer to the government's power to regulate, to control pollution and to minimize waste. If one examines the clauses one cannot help but be satisfied that this bill contains the power to ensure that the benefits from our national resources can accrue to the Canadian people. The real question that arises on an examination of this bill is not in respect of the technical competence of the bill to do the job but whether we will have a government whose policy will be in harmony with, the purpose of this bill only then will we avoid a future sell-out of our natural resources such as we have had in the past. No bill can guarantee that a sell-out of this kind does not take place. That depends on government policy and the willingness of government to act in the best interests of the Canadian people.
This could be very good legislation. I have only one caveat to enter. Clause 6 which appears on page 4 of the bill, reads as follows:
No member of the Committee shall have a pecuniary interest of any description, directly
April IS, 1969	COMMONS
or indirectly, in any property in oil or gas to which this Act applies or own shares in any company engaged in any phase of the oil or gas industry in Canada in an amount in excess of five per cent of the issued shares thereof.
It strikes me that 5 per cent of the shares can very frequently amount to a controlling interest and anyone holding that percentage of shares who acted on the committee could have a conflict of interests. I would think that particular limitation should be removed. I do not think there should be any question of a conflict of interest for those who serve on the board. I think they should be divorced from any pecuniary attachment outside their work.
The provisions of this bill strike me as being somewhat better than those contained in provincial statutes of a similar nature. They take into account the tragic waste of capital and resources that has occurred because conditions were not laid down in the early days of oil development in Canada. We are still suffering from the failure of provincial governments to lay down guide lines in this direction. In fairness to the provincial governments it must be pointed out that for a long time the oil industry was able to bargain and say in effect that it would go along with whoever would give the best deal. The provincial governments may have had limited ability to stand up to the international giants in the oil industry. It is obvious that this kind of inability does not apply to the federal government. The federal government cannot be bargained off in the way the provincial governments were. Therefore, the federal government can be expected to take a much firmer stand.
There is one area in which the federal government has been very remiss. It has stood by or has actively encouraged wasteful expenditures in the oil industry. The Carter commission pointed out that the depletion allowances which exist in our present tax structure have encouraged more investment in the industry than market forces or any kind of forces, or indeed any intelligent planning, would have indicated to be desirable. The commission pointed out that the special privileges for the oil industry should be removed for two very good reasons. First, the Canadian people are entitled to obtain a reasonable tax from those who use the natural resources of the country. Secondly, this would discourage some of the wasteful investment that has taken place in the oil industry.
At the moment when we are considering oil, we must think beyond its effect on the northern areas of Canada. The whole situation seems to be up in the air. The question
DEBATES	7547
Oil and Gas Production and Conservation of our exports to the United States seem to be somewhat in doubt. It might be useful to look back on Canada's national oil policy, how it came into being and some of the effects of that national oil policy. One cannot help but feel that this national oil policy was not written by the legislators of Canada but was written largely by the international oil companies themselves to suit their particular purpose. A story is told about the way the concessions were wrung from the international oil companies, even the minor concessions which were obtained from them. The Canadian government wanted greater access from the United States market for its oil. The government threatened to build a pipe line to Montreal. The international oil companies opted in favour of a continental oil policy of a type rather than a Canadian National Policy. They responded to a threat from the government of the day and I suspect from one minister in particular.
At this crucial moment it may be necessary for this government to state in no uncertain terms that it is prepared to exercise such a threat again unless a better arrangement is made for the oil industry of this country. It might be best perhaps for the oil industry, and for the nation as a whole, not to even threaten the building of a pipe line to Montreal but to go ahead and do it anyway simply because it might, in the long run, give us a more stable future than has been the case in the past. We paid quite a price for that deal with the international oil companies. The agreement was that Canadian oil would flow as far as the Ottawa River and that the oil needs east of that point would be served by off-shore oil. Although never officially stated, I believe the understanding was that the offshore oil displaced in the United States would be taken in at the port of Montreal.
By going along with this agreement Canada, in effect, made itself part and parcel of United States foreign policy and part and parcel of the international oil companies' arrangements with countries that were friendly to the United States. I am not aware that this parliament was ever told this was the deal or that this was the situation. Only in the years subsequent to the development of the national oil policy have some of these facts become more clear.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
After all the benefits of this vaunted oil policy have been counted, where do we stand today? First of all, we still have a great
April 15. 1969
7548	COMMONS
Oil and Gas Production and Conservation imbalance in respect of oil in that we are importing more than we export, despite the fact we are capable of not only supplying all Canadian needs but probably the needs of the United States as well. We have a tremendous capacity in this country. Our exploration costs and our cost of oil recovery are somewhat lower than those in the United States, although perhaps higher than the cost in countries in the Middle East or Venezuela. Our exploration and recovery costs are about i lower than those in the United States, yet our prices are among the highest in the world, if not the highest to the consumer.
Someone might say that gasoline costs $1 per gallon in France, but I am referring to the price less tax. We in Canada are paying a higher price for gasoline, less tax, than anyone in any country in the world, and there is no need for this situation. One individual sent me an estimate in which it was suggested that the Canadian consumer was paying approximately $500 million more each year for gasoline than necessary. We have put ourselves in the position of being scared to death about what the United States might do regarding the importation of oil from Canada.
Day after day in this house we have seen concerned members from the West rising to ask the government what is to happen in respect of our exportation of oil to the United States. I can appreciate that western members are concerned about this matter because a great deal of the prosperity and orientation of our western provinces is related to the exportation of oil. It always gripes me to note that these questions are asked with an almost pathetic feeling accompanied by a fear about what we would do if the United States cut off our oil exports. Apparently we should do everything possible to ensure our access to the oil market of the United States.
This situation is a dreadful one for any country and we must find a solution. It is time that we developed a truly Canadian oil policy which made long term sense and put us in a position other than that of a satellite of the United States, subject to the whims and pleasures of lobbying or the changed nature of United States politics.
A number of studies have been conducted in respect of the feasibility of a pipeline to Montreal. Some of these studies were conducted privately and some publicly. Most of them contain arguments that at the present cost of offshore and domestic crude, and the cost of transportation, such a pipeline would not be feasible but would tend to increase the


price of gasoline on the Montreal market unless the market were protected. '
These arguments are based on a number of factors. First of all, they assume that the price of crude in Canada at the wellhead is a correct price and that there is no reason to doubt that this price is as low as it might be. These arguments are based on the belief that this price is a realistic one and not related to the United States market. It can be demonstrated that the price of Canadian crude could be substantially lowered, still leaving sufficient profit to those people in the oil industry.
The price of crude oil at Montreal delivered through a pipeline is sometimes based on the cost of transporting oil through privately owned pipelines. The cost of transporting this oil through a publicly owned pipeline has not been calculated. The only figure I have heard as to the difference between the cost of transporting by a privately owned pipeline in comparison with a publicly owned pipeline was the figure given to us at a committee hearing a number of years ago. At that time we asked a member of the energy board whether this would make a difference. He said there would be a considerable reduction in cost as between publicly and privately owned companies. If we are to move crude oil to Montreal it seems we must do so through a publicly owned pipeline.
From all the evidence I have seen, I am convinced that we could probably reduce the cost of crude oil in Canada if we operated publicly owned pipelines rather than the jumble of privately owned pipelines which now exist.

It is my belief that a publicly owned pipeline can be shown to be more economic than one operated privately, providing there are flow guarantees. Let me read from a report of a commission set up by a privately owned, independent oil producer association in Canada in respect of the outlook for Canadien crude, production and marketing. The consultant was W. S. Levy and Company Incorporated. This report refers to the Montreal market and reads:
If access to the Montreal market permitted accelerated production of Canadian crude, the producing industry could take a considerable reduction in crude prices without economic loss. For example, with a 200,000 barrel per day increase in production, crude prices could be around 22 cents per barrel lower without any reduction in the present discounted value of future production, even taking a 5 per cent discount factor. And transportation costs to Montreal might be reduced by perhaps 13 cents per barrel, if substantial volumes of Canadian crude were to be moved to Montreal, in addition to the increasing volume into eastern Ontario.
The report concludes:
The Montreal market is a less economically attractive alternative. But if Canada's expanding productive potential cannot achieve adequate volume in U.S. markets, or if prolonged uncertainty seriously threatens incentives to Canadian oil development the entry of Canadian oil into Montreal could be considered as an alternative. At least to the extent that the preferred alternative of expanding exports proves elusive, the preference for low priced foreign oil in Montreal might also have to be qualified.
The argument is sometimes advanced that if we try to move Canadian crude into Montreal the international corporations which own oil wells in Canada, in Venezuela and the Middle East would cut their prices at the port of Montreal to make sure that it would be uneconomic to transport Canadian oil to that market. They would not be cutting their price, they would be maintaining the price to meet the cost of Canadian crude.
We are not getting any benefit from free entry of oil at Montreal. These companies are adjusting their prices to make sure that the cost of oil at Montreal will enable them to maintain this privileged position. This position is supported by our national oil policy. I think the real question, therefore, as it concerns oil in Canada, is whether this parliament, acting on behalf of the people of our country, will determine the nature and future of the oil industry in the best interests of Canadians, or whether we will permit the international oil companies to do what they think is best in their own interests.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I hold no brief for any particular industry, but I think it is high time somebody from western Canada set out the case for western Canada. We have been talking about the north, and I link what I have to say with the arguments put forward. We have been dealing with exploration in the north and the effect it will have on other oil and petroleum pools and energy resources in Canada, particularly western Canada.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) went to Calgary to speak about the petroleum industry-perhaps I can say this better than most other members who have knowledge of the subject-he did not speak to the people who have knowledge, experience and financial interest in the industry. I do not refer only to the companies but to the people of Alberta. The industry pours a large amount of money into the treasury because we are the only province without a sales tax. I think that even my own friends to the left would see some economic advantage in this.
The Prime Minister did not speak to the oil industry about their problems with regard to trade. Why was this? The reason is that the Prime Minister went to see the President of the United States-he had with him several briefcases' of documents concerning various subjects-and left the impression in Washington that we in Canada were going to pull out of the collective defence of the western world. He met with the President of the United States, the Presidents' advisers and his cabinet members. When the President of the United States was vice-president of that great country he had some sympathy for Canada, but on this occasion he had little sympathy for the Prime Minister's arguments with reference to Canadian trade in petroleum and wheat, because of our attitude in reference to NATO.
I think the President of the United States told the Prime Minister that we were not interested in measuring up to our responsibilities as a nation to work with the western world. One can only negotiate with the other side of the world from a position of strength, not weakness. We are taking the French, de Gaulle, line with reference to defence. During the election campaign the Prime Minister told the United States that we would pull right out of NATO. This is the reason he received such little sympathy for Canada's problems in the petroleum and wheat industries. I use wheat only as an analogy. We are already

Canadian National Railways and Air Canada down 60 per cent in our production. I spoke about this great industry over a year and a half ago and warned the government what would happen to our wheat trade and petroleum trade if they did not immediately come to grips with these problems.
I think this is the message the Prime Minister of Canada got from the President of the United States, because he came back here and said-he was speaking metaphorically, of course-that dealing with the United States was like sleeping with a big elephant. He should have said, in view of the advice he received regarding international policy, that he felt like a mouse caught in the toe of the elephant.
We on this side of the house have for many years been asking questions in order to ascertain where Canada is going as far as the north is concerned. One of the problems is, of course, where is the northern boundary? This problem was not created by this government or parliament. I would be most selfish if I laid responsibility for the problems concerning the boundary of the north on this government. I say this because on July 24, 1964, I asked the following question which can be found at page 5941 of Hansard. The question had been asked before in this House of Commons. I asked:
Could I ask the minister one question? It may be this is not the proper time to deal with it, and perhaps the hon. gentleman would like to answer it later.
Could the minister give some indication to the house, because of the stress on the importance of the north-
I emphasize that this was five years ago.
-whether there is a definite northern border in Canada: and could he tell us how many oceanographers and other scientists are working at the present time in defining a true northern boundary for Canada? It seems to me very important that this should be done, particularly with the type of world in which we are now living.
The Minister said he could not answer the question but would look into it. These matters are very important when we are dealing with a bill which will affect the great, wealthy resources of petroleum that are to be found in the northern islands of Canada. In this respect we have a conflict with the United States. If our border does stretch to the far northern islands, we are only twelve miles from the U.S.S.R.

speechtext:
In the few minutes I had before supper I pointed out that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) went to the United States for consultations with the United States President and his advisers with a view to obtaining a better deal for the petroleum and oil industry as well as for our wheat trade he ran into some difficulty because, in my personal opinion, Canada had failed to live up to its responsibility, so far as the western world is concerned, for the collective defence of the western world. As I suggested before supper, when the Prime Minister said that dealing with the United States was like sleeping with an elephant he probably felt like a mouse caught in the toe of the elephant because he was being squeezed to death as a result of the prejudice to our foreign policy.
I also mentioned the fact that the question of our northern boundary is not a new one. It has been discussed on many occasions. I myself raised the question on July 24, 1964, when I asked the then minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, Mr. Laing:
-could the minister give some indication to the house, because of the stress on the importance of the north, whether there is a definite northern border in Canada; and could he tell us how many oceanographers and other scientists are working at the present time in defining a true northern boundary for Canada?
At that time we were promised an answer, but have not received one yet. This was almost five years ago, and we are still in the same dilemma. We really do not know today where our northern boundary is. This matter is becoming increasingly important in view of the now known and proven reserve of petroleum, our wealthy resources and our mines. I recall my words as they appear at page 5960 of Hansard of July 24, 1964. At that time the committee of the whole was discussing the estimates of the department of northern affairs, and during that debate I said the following:
Mr. Chairman, before going on with a few suggestions in regard to the parks, I would like to say something with regard to northern affairs. I have here a map of Canada which shows Melville Island, Hubert Island, and so on, away up to Alert Point. I have just been told by the hon. member for Northwest Territories that Alert Point is 2,350 miles north of Winnipeg.
7551
Oil and Gas Production and Conservation
I pointed out that the distance from Calgary to Ottawa is 2,600 miles, so it is almost as far from Winnipeg to Alert Point as it is from Ottawa to Calgary. We appreciate therefore, how vast is the north. I also said:
I have said that it is 2,400 miles from Alert Point to Winnipeg. This is a vast area of our country. We have heard the hon. member for Yukon on several occasions; we have heard the minister and others talk about the vast resources of the north. Those resources are there. Let us make sure they stay Canadian. To do this we should now take a serious look at the matter of establishing our northern boundary. I put this suggestion forward as a constructive suggestion-
Yet, five years later there are members on this side of the house asking the Prime Minister whether the government is concerned with the 'delineation of our northern boundary. We wonder whether the islands I have mentioned, which contain a proven reserve of oil and a vast quantity of valuable minerals, are within that boundary.
I also said that a case should be made for the west. It seems to me it is high time that some of us from western Canada spoke up for the west. As I said before the supper hour, we have already lost the wheat market. Our exports are down by 60 per cent, and I predict tonight as I predicted before, that we are now about to lose our oil markets. Every day when we question the government we receive the same answers that the matter is being reviewed, that it is being considered, and that task forces are being set up.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
The reason the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) did not discuss the subject of petroleum in the City of Calgary is not unrelated with the position he took with regard to NATO and similar areas where he had to deal collectively with the western world. In such matters we can never make a decision ourselves; we can only negotiate from strength. Hence the weakness of the case the Prime Minister presented in Washington. This is what the Gazette had to say about the oil situation as early as October 28, 1968:
Canadian deliveries of crude oil east of the Rockies for October will run around 275,000 barrels daily or under the U.S. suggested ceiling of 280,000, sources here say.
I wonder what the reaction would be in central Canada, the centre of power, where we find the largest number of parliamentary seats. Canada is an anomaly in the world today. It can currently produce over 200 per cent of its current rate of consumption and yet has a net trade deficit in oil of over $200

April 15. 1969
7552	COMMONS
Oil and Gas Production and Conservation million per year. The need lor a new oil policy is apparent-that is, a policy which adequately recognizes the new developments which have taken place ini recent years and the changes which can be expected to occur in the future.
When anybody talks about petroleum today and the national oil policy created by this party when we were in government, he should realize that the policy then set up is as dead today as Marley's ghost. The only reason there is any trade between the two countries today is because that trade is a bit like Topsy. The United States is dictating to Canada, and proper consultation is not taking place because this government is failing to measure up to its responsibility.
What is the effect of all this? Let us talk about grain for a few moments. It is not only western Canada that is suffering as a result of the difficulties facing that industry. When I spoke in Dresden, Ontario 800 men had just been laid off by the International Harvester plant. I understand how some hon. members think about this subject, but somebody has to present the case for the west. We hear it said: They had it good for a number of years. The fact is we are not dealing exclusively with western Canada but with the economy of Canada as a whole. The same holds true when I speak of the petroleum industry. We only produce in western Canada some 40 or 50 per cent of the amount we are capable of producing, taking into account all the rules and regulations in respect of conservation. If the $200 million presently spent on imports were spent in Canada for Canadian crude oil, the total effect on the Canadian economy through secondary and tertiary industries would be approximately $700 million annually. At present we have a trade deficit because, among other things, we are purchasing $200 million worth of crude petroleum from abroad.
Major Canadian banking institutions have calculated that the multiplier effect of money generated in the national resource sector of our economy is approximately 3.3. Canada loses on every barrel of imported crude oil, not only through the foreign production profits which remain offshore, but because each barrel of Canadian crude oil pays more than one dollar in the form of taxes and other payments to Canadian governments. Therefore, to the extent of Canada's crude oil imports, such revenue is lost. Replacement of such imports by Canadian oil would result in

Oil and Gas Production and Conservation and the United States that have grown in the past decade of expanding western Canadian oil potential, declining United States oil security and increasing uncertainties of oil supplies.
Prudhoe, and the expanding Canada oil search, have made a new ball game, and new ground rules are needed. Economic interests of Canada and the United States, continued adequate growth of reserves and security demand that the North American nations and their oilmen gather facts, bargain hard, and evolve new continental guidelines. The faster that is done, the sooner will Arctic resources join others on the continent in creating an economically secure energy supply for the growing hunger of years ahead.
With the reserves not only in Alaska but in the Arctic, in northern Canada and on the plains, the oil market should be prorated so that everybody gets a percentage. In our national oil policy a deal was struck with the United States. My good friend from the New Democratic party said this afternoon that we should not make deals like this, but you cannot live in economic isolation. The deal we made was that we would permit Venezuelan crude petroleum to come into Canada as far as the Ottawa valley, serving the concentrated population areas of eastern Canada, providing the United States would let us have a certain percentage of the northwest market down to Chicago and Toledo.
Why did we make that deal, Mr. Speaker? First of all, it was to secure a fair market for Canada, rewarding those people who had invested their money in this country as well as assisting the growth of the industry. We also made this deal because we knew, as did the United States, that in order to keep both North America and South America free from a Communist revolution we would have to encourage trade. Therefore, this deal was struck to permit Venezuelan crude to come to eastern Canada, thus keeping trade between Venezuela and Canada and Venezuela and the United States in a healthy condition. That is the real reason behind the national oil policy, but as I have said it is now as dead as Mar-ley's ghost.
On top of this we now have this tremendous development in the north, with the serious possibility that in the near future Alberta, Saskatchewan and even Manitoba will be bypassed as far as markets for natural gas and crude petroleum are concerned. We on this side of the house say that it is high time that the government brought in a new oil

policy. It is high time the government negotiated with the United States and advised parliament of their decision. But this government never seems to learn. It is a cabinet government that does not know that parliament is the place to seek information, to make suggestions, as I am now doing, suggestions that have been prompted by the serious nature of the events now taking place in western Canada.
I repeat that as far as the west is concerned, having lost our agricultural markets we are now about to lose our petroleum markets. Depressed economic conditions are, sowing the seeds of the formation of a new splinter party, a party now seen to be sprouting in the west,-and let us be realistic and face it-that leans towards separation from this nation. Who has sat in this chamber for a period of time, even for the period that I have sat here, and does not believe that Canada is a great nation that can only be held together when we all appreciate each other's economic problems from the mari-times to Victoria?
The Prudhoe Bay development means that the great trio of North American oil states is becoming a quartet, spread from the Arctic to the Gulf coast. Number one is Texas, with proved petroleum reserves of about 19 billion barrels. Its gulf neighbour, Louisiana, is approaching nine billion, slightly behind Canada's Alberta in the heart of the continent. Prudhoe could give Alaska over the next year or two as much as 10 billion barrels proved. And northern Canada could make up a quintet soon after. In fact, "oil giants" need not stop at five.
Prudhoe came at a time when exploration was already spreading in Canada beyond the Alberta heartland into geologically favourable regions across the nation. Stimulated by Prudhoe, the Canadian play now covers over one billion acres, over 1.5 million square miles, under exploration permit or lease.
We heard this afternoon that we had encouraged too much investment in developing the petroleum industry. Surely we cannot have too much capital to develop this kind of resource. We need all the capital we can get to develop these resources and markets so that we can balance our trade with other countries, increase our gross national product and not have to go to the little wage earner for more taxes. We must increase the industrial growth of this nation, and that is where I part company with the Socialists. I cannot understand their arguments. Fancy having an

April 15, 1969
Oil and Gas Production and Conservation hon. member say this afternoon that there is too much investment in Canada in the development of oil! If we adopt that kind of thinking, Canada will remain forever in the dark ages.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
May I now say a word about natural gas. There has been tremendous development in the last few years in this field and western Canada needs more secondary industry. Natural gas is being piped from western Canada to eastern Canada and the United States. We do not have in our area concentrated centres of population. We ought to develop secondary industry so that western Canada could use, as a raw material the available natural gas. Certainly, our natural gas will enable secondary industry to be established in our area and the entire nation will benefit economically.
My last thoughts are these, Mr. Speaker. I note that not many government supporters are here. I plead with the government, nevertheless, to come forward with some petroleum policy which will answer our needs. If the minister does not think Canada is ready to negotiate a new continental oil policy wouldi it not be more honest for the government to come to the house and tell us the truth, so that our people may know the truth. He should be honest with us instead of hiding the facts and talking about establishing task forces and conducting reviews.
Not only should we be advised of the truth of the situation, as we ought to have been advised by the minister some months ago with respect to the grain industry, but the minister ought to tell us exactly what the government's approach to this problem is. I ask the minister to consider setting up a committee composed of hon. members of this house and of the other place so that we may talk with congressmen in the United States, set before them Canada's position and try to work out a new continental oil policy under which Canada gets a square deal in the North American petroleum market. The taxes that this industry can pay will be enormous and could go towards establishing secondary industries in this nation.
The economic health of central Canada is not good. I expect that the other hon. member for Calgary will make a plea similar to mine. I expect he will advocate that we take a new look at the petroleum industry. I have always said that we westerners must stick together. Our differences in this house stem from the
differences in the areas we represent rather than from any political differences. I have always maintained that. It has always been, a rule in this house that one stands to talk and sits to listen. For too long has this country taken the idea for granted that everything in western Canada is extravagantly wealthy and that we are living ini luxury. Our agricultural industry faces its most severe crisis since the 1930's. In western Canada we are moving toward a recession the like of which has not been seen since the 1930's and the petroleum industry also will soon move into a recession. One is always proud when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) visits one's city, but I say to the government that the reception he received the other night will be as nothing to the one he will receive six months from now if he does not make a very clear and honest effort to improve the situation of the people of western Canada. I say to the government that we are on the move. If we do not get help here we shall get it elsewhere.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish I could share the feelings of hon. members who congratulated the minister early today for introducing this legislation. They said it was timely legislation. Frankly, I had hoped that by this time we would see tremendous oil discoveries in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon and that this legislation would be late in coming. We have been disappointed in this regard, and the legislation is timely.
The first oil and gas conservation legislation in Canada was enacted in the province of Alberta in 1938 and our basic conservation concepts have remained much the same. They are, to effect the conservation of oil and gas resources, to prevent their waste, to secure the observance of sufficient and efficient practices in the location, spacing, drilling, equipping as well as the operating and abandonment of wells. In short, that concept covers all aspects of the production of oil and gas. Another aim of our legislation is to afford the owner of the producing property his just and equitable share of the production of any pool.
As I say, this legislation was pioneered in Alberta. We had the benefit of experience in the United States and we did not have the benefit of any experience in Canada. It is interesting to note some of the similarities and differences in the present legislation and legislation which was pioneered in Alberta. That legislation, incidentally, formed the
7556	COMMONS
Oil and Gas Production and Conservation basis for the Norwegian government's legislation after petroleum had been found under the North Sea adjacent to that country.
In Alberta we have a mixture of freehold and Crown lands. In the Northwest Territories mineral rights are all vested in the Crown. In Alberta, the Oil and Gas Conservation Board is a body corporate and in the proposed legislation it will be a committee serving under the minister. In Alberta, the operations of the Board are financed by the province and by private owners. Under the proposed legislation the operations of the committee will be entirely government financed. In Alberta, the Board controls its own expenditures, has the authority to hire its own staff and determine what facilities it requires. Under the proposed legislation, the committee will be dependent entirely on the minister and on Treasury Board.
All these differences, I take it, stem from the basic fact that in that province we have freehold and Crown land whereas here we are dealing entirely with Crown land; and there can be no objection in principle to these differences. There is one distinction in this proposed legislation which I think is remarkably progressive. The Conservation Boards or members of Conservation Boards of the various provinces are entirely appointed by the Lieutenant Governors in Council. Under this legislation, we are to have a five man committee, and two of those men must be from outside the public service. Furthermore, one of those two outside members must be present at any meeting in order to make a quorum. That is something the petroleum industry has been urging for a long time in the province of Alberta. I am very happy to see that the federal government has taken the initiative and got off on the right foot by implementing this suggestion immediately.
The hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Salts-man) was worried in case one of those outside members might have some interest in the petroleum industry. I think he referred to the provisions of clause 6. I take it that clause 6 provides they may have no direct interest in any oil plans over which the committee would have jurisdiction, but they may have an interest in the petroleum industry or a company connected with the petroleum industry in Canada. I feel it would be very difficult in this particular industry to obtain the services of the type of competent person that will be required on this board. Almost any person who is the least bit knowledgeable in

DEBATES	April 15, 1969
the industry has some investment in it. That is one of the nice things about it.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
We are not talking about an industry that is looked at remotely as some people who advocate nationalized industries tend to observe them. This is an industry in which almost everyone who is the least bit successful has a very intimate and particular concern with what they are doing. I have dealt at some length with the act and do not want to be any more particular. This is not the time to do that.
I was very interested in the brief survey of the oil discoveries in the area that this will cover which the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras) gave. He pointed out that the only oil in that area to date is the Norman Wells discovery which was made in the early years of the war. There are numerous small gas pools and more recently a large gas pool was discovered. Those small gas pools may be small by standards of the Northwest Territories, but the fact is the ones there today would very definitely be commercial reserves were they located closer to markets than they are.
I do not think from what we have in the way of discoveries there can be any doubt in the long run we are going to have a major gas industry in the Northwest Territories. About two weeks ago a $1.4 billion project to pipe gas from the Liard River Valley and from portions of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan was announced. For the first time, gas from the Northwest Territories will be going into the United States midwest market.
While the people at Prudhoe Bay may contemplate building a pipe line across Alaska and sending the oil across the west coast to market, there is no way they can economically move gas that way. The gas that comes out of prudhoe Bay will have to come down the coast of the Arctic Ocean, down the Mackenzie River valley and through the western provinces to the United States.
Gas is something that has been rather neglected by people talking about the oil and petroleum problems of western Canada. In 1957 the United States imported about 60 million cubic feet of Canadian natural gas per day. By 1968 this volume increased to 1,570 million cubic feet per day, approximately 2,500 per cent. This year it is anticipated it will reach approximately 1,800 million cubic
April 15, 1969


water resources for a long, long time. I do not want to impair the negotiations at all but I am hopeful that in taking a look at the overall energy situation on this continent all forms of energy will be included because, if so, we have a great deal to sell the United States which cannot be supplied by Prudhoe Bay or by other parts of the United States.

subtopic: MEASURE ESTABLISHING OIL AND GAS COMMITTEE, AND REGULATING POWERS OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased that Bill S-29 is before us and that the government is taking this step in bringing some order to the petroleum industry, particularly as it affects the new frontier of the north. I do not think the importance of this bill can be over-estimated. However, I do not believe we really understand how important it is. As has been said today by the former minister of northern affairs in the Diefenbaker administration, a great step forward has been made in the north and the vision has caught on. But it has not entirely caught on yet. The people of Canada still do not appreciate the whole purport of what will happen if we do not take immediate steps to grasp the opportunities which exist. In some cases this may be the last opportunity we will have for perhaps 25 years. This great new resource which has been discovered, particularly on the shores of the Arctic, is extremely important. It will have a great effect on the settled areas of the three prairie provinces.
If we are not very careful our great opportunity to take part in this new development will slip through our fingers. Instead of being a great opportunity for Canadians to take advantage of this new development, it may well be a crippling blow to our own petroleum industry for a period up to 25 years. I would suggest that because we have no merchant fleet of any note we should get cracking on a pipe line, not just a pipe line but perhaps many pipe lines. If we supply the facilities first to move this oil rapidly and cheaply to the heart of the north American continent, we will have a great deal to say about the industries which will spring up along those pipe lines. In this way we may be able to compete with the cheap ocean traffic which we know is a great threat to any other form of transportation on this planet. I would like to see us build ships, but I think it is too late now to recall the warnings we had over the past 20 years in respect of Canada's merchant shipping. So, I am limited to the very narrow point of begging that we get cracking on an oil policy for Canada so that we will
April 15, 1969
have the ability to move this oil to the continental markets of the United States.
If we have this ability to move the oil and gas, we will derive the benefit of the employment which will result from the building of the lines. In addition, frontier towns will spring up. We will not only have the benefit of these lines but also of the industry which will grow up along these pipe lines for the next 100 years. If we do not do this, we will lose this industry.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
I have seen editorials in newspapers throughout the United States and across this country which indicate that Alaskan authorities are worried about this very thing. These people want to build up a great sea-going complex. They want to build a great Arctic port to handle this oil on behalf of this country. If we build this series of pipe lines which I envisage we can help develop our own reserves.
It is not only Prudhoe Bay that is rich in oil. We have every reason to believe that Prudhoe Bay is only a small part of a much larger field which stretches throughout the Canadian north, the Arctic islands and the ocean beds which are close to Canadian soil. It is expected that these reserves will prove within the next 25 years to be so large as to dwarf the Prudhoe Bay potentiality. It is only through the establishment of pipelines that we can expect to handle this development. This is our opportunity and we must move quickly.
It is my hope that the government will not listen to those on my extreme left who advocate the development of this area on the basis of a government monopoly. People living in high rise apartments in large cities must have a source of income. We must make some claim to cut in the people of Canada on this development. We must work out an ideal situation closely tied with our tax structure to encourage these people, particularly the young, to take advantage of this opportunity to go north during the summer months, These people who are attending university could well spend these few months exploring this area and constructing these pipelines. We should encourage them to do so through tax incentives. Perhaps we should provide a five year tax moratorium in order to develop this area while at the same time helping these young people to finish university. This would amount to an investment in this country. The experience would be an advantage to these 29180-479
Oil and Gas Production and Conservation young people when they are living in high rise apartments in large cities. These people must have an income greater than what they might receive from relief. This is a new frontier and it needs developing.
This new development represents something greater than the biggest gold rush of our time. I have in mind the oil reserves in the Northwest Territories, the Arctic and those areas adjacent to this country. These areas are also rich in copper deposits and those water resources to which the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Mahoney) has referred. We must take into account not only the oil reserves and an oil policy but also a transportation policy. We must provide transportation facilities in the north, particularly along the Mackenzie River. Perhaps the best way to do this is by building pipelines.
When I first came to this house 11 years ago, I was aware of the tremendous value of the tar sands in northern Alberta. I am afraid these will not be developed for a number of years but they will still exist after we have taken the oil from the Arctic islands. This resource remains for future development but such development will require vision and encouragement. We must now grasp this vision of northern development, and we must do something about it.
I could not agree more than I do with my confrere, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), when he suggests1 that we cannot expect the United States to co-operate with us on an economic basis unless we in turn co-operate with the United States both economically and ideologically. I believe that we are much closer in agreement with the ideology of the United States than ideologies held by other countries. Our future depends on the joint security of North America.
Those ideals held by free countries in Europe upon which we relied are no longer reliable. These countries are now vulnerable. If we stand with our friends here in North America we may well find that in the year 2000 this area will be strong and free. We in this country must be prepared, as a part of North America, to defend ourselves. We must co-operate in this regard with the United States. We must not make this country a haven for those individuals who run away from their duties south of the border. We must do something more than criticize. We must prove that we are willing to enter the 21st century on a bargaining basis backed up by more than just rich natural resources, tremendous water power, fresh water resources,

subtopic: MEASURE ESTABLISHING OIL AND GAS COMMITTEE, AND REGULATING POWERS OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up too much of the time of the house. I have listened with interest to the various speakers and am rather surprised at some of the speeches I have heard. We have had a speech on defence policy. I have searched the bill in vain to find a clause dealing with defence policy. However, I presume that quite a bit of latitude is allowed in this type of debate and I accept the speeches in that spirit.
Bill S-29, an act respecting the production and conservation of oil and gas in the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories, is an important piece of legislation. Having checked through the bill, I find it is divided basically into four sections. I would like to very briefly deal with each section and then ask a few questions regarding the oil and gas policy of the Liberal government. I think I know what their gas policy is; we have had a great deal of that since September. But the Canadian people are entitled to a very clear blueprint of where we are going in the development of this extremely important resource.
The bill we are discussing this evening is an interesting piece of legislation which could have a very decided influence on the production and conservation of oil and gas, particularly in the Yukon and Northwest Territories. This is the main function of the bill, as I understand it. Gas and oil resources are primarily the responsibility of the provincial authorities. That is why this bill applies
DEBATES	7561
Oil and Gas Production and Conservation primarily to the Northwest Territories and the Yukon.
A close examination of the bill will disclose that most of the regulations for the production and conservation of our oil and gas resources have been left to the Governor in Council. This seems to be one of the long suits of this government, namely, orders in council and regulations which are left to the cabinet. I believe this is one of the major weaknesses in the proposed legislation. You can lay down good guide lines, but those good guide lines can be utterly destroyed by a legislative group which sets up regulations which are not in the interests of the industry or the people of Canada. I, for one, feel that provincially and federally we have had far too much government by order in council and not enough legislation is contained in the bills which we pass.
As I said before, the bill is divided into four main parts. One section sets up the oil and gas committee which will consist of five members, not more than three of whom will be from the public service. I think this is a good section of the bill. The committee will oversee the production and conservation of oil and gas in the Yukon and Northwest Territories. It is provided in the bill that to be a member of the committee one must have specialized or technical knowledge of the oil and gas industry. Again, I think this is an essential ingredient of such a member of the Committee.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Then, the bill defines the exemptions of those who are allowed to sit on the board. The clause reads:
No member of the Committee shall have a pecuniary interest of any description, directly or indirectly, in any profit in oil or gas to which this Act applies or own shares in any company engaged in any phase of the oil or gas industry in Canada in an amount in excess of five per cent of the issued shares thereof.
Sometimes when I look at this last qualification I am not certain that it is a good one. Many of these companies are closely tied together, and some of them are subsidiaries. This is something about which we must be very careful.
On checking the legislation I find that the committee is all powerful. It can hold inquiries and hear appeals about various matters. It has the power, the rights and privileges of a superior court of record. Its findings on any
7562	COMMONS
Oil and Gas Production and Conservation questions of fact are binding and conclusive. Clause 11 reads:
Any order made by the Committee may, for the purpose of enforcement thereof, be made an order of the Exchequer Court of Canada-
Of course, I must add that at the end of the bill there is a clause dealing with appeals, and this is essential in any legislation. There must be an appeal from bad decisions made by the government, and they make plenty of them. We find that part I of the bill deals with the production and conservation of our gas and oil resources. This is where the regulations come in, and this is where I believe Canadians should be more apprehensive than ever because all the regulating and defining is left in this particular part of the bill.
Members of this house do not know what is to be put in the regulations, and I for one would be very anxious to have the minister give us, if not on second reading at least in the committee stage, far more detail than he gave to the house this afternoon in moving the second reading of the bill. I think we, and the Canadian people, are entitled to this information.
I notice that part II of the bill defines "waste". It empowers the chief conservation officer to prevent it and also allows an appeal from the decision of the chief conservation officer to the committee if a decision is made by him which the company or the individuals concerned do not like.
We find that part II deals with production arrangements. This section of the bill regulates the economic and efficient production of oil and gas from the areas affected. I believe this is good legislation. It is too bad that such legislation containing proper controls was not introduced many years ago by all the provinces. In my opinion, the clauses dealing with pooling arrangements and unitization agreements seem to be in line with sound conservation policies. But again I say this ties in with the regulations which should be set by order in council and of which the house at this time has no knowledge.
Part III of the bill deals with appeals and administration. However, we find again that the Governor in Council may at any time vary or rescind any decision or order of the committee. In my opinion, this does not make for good legislation.
Many hon. members who have taken part in the debate have dealt with the export of Canadian oil and we have had a good discussion on the existing potential in Canada, so I will not go over these points again. There is

DEBATES	April 15, 1969
just one aspect which a number of hon. members did not touch upon, that is the degree of ownership of the oil and gas resources of this country. Over the years I have been very apprehensive on seeing Canadian resources gradually pass from Canadian control into foreign hands. This is where I believe that we as Canadians must re-examine our position with regard to resource ownership.
Last December I asked some questions in the house regarding the percentage of ownership in this industry. I would like to put the figures on record. For petroleum and gas wells the assets held by foreign controlled companies at the end of 1965 amounted to 83.6 per cent of the total, and the assets held by Canadian controlled companies amounted to 16.4 per cent of the total. These figures show that Canadian control has been lost in this sector of the industry.
Then, we come to petroleum refineries. This is another very important sector of this great industry. Here, we find that the assets held by foreign controlled companies at the end of 1965 amounted to 99 per cent of the total in Canada, and 1 per cent was held by Canadian companies.
Next we come to pipe lines, and here the picture is a little brighter. We find that foreign control was 26.8 per cent while Canadian control was 73.2 per cent.
Then, we come to the marketing of petroleum and gas products, and I presume this refers to the little gas stations which we find on the corner of nearly every street. Here again we find that the Canadian control in this instance was 81.5 per cent, while foreign control was 18.5 per cent. However, it is to be noted that the petroleum resources and the refining of petroleum is mainly under the control of those who live outside the boundaries of our nation. I think that this is not good so far as Canadian control of this resource is concerned.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
There are a few questions which I should like to put to the minister in connection with our oil policy. I think every speaker this afternoon and this evening stressed the problem of marketing. I think this problem is one of the major factors in the development of our oil and gas resources. This is why I should like to direct a question or two to the minister. We have heard a great deal about Panarctic Oil. Here, a corporation has been set up to go into the northern part of Canada, and the
April 15, 1969	COMMONS
government itself is participating in the venture. The government has put up money and its representatives sit on the board of directors of the corporation. This development is a very interesting aspect of Canadian life and it is time the minister gave us some clear information about it. He could tell us what we are doing and, in general, how many acres are under the control of Canadian companies; how much of this vast potential oil acreage in the north is under the control of companies outside this nation and just what the government intends to do about marketing the products in the north. I have read a great deal about this. In fact, I have volumes of information or speculation by various writers who stress the fantastic cost of oil production in the north and draw attention to the difficulty of getting the product to markets in the south, in the west or in Europe.
We must be given some answers to these questions. Does the government have a plan foir the sensible marketing of this product once sufficient pools of oil have been found? Are pipe lines to be built? Is there a plan which hon. members can see? Can the Canadian people be taken into the confidence of the department? This type of information is required by members here and by the Canadian public at large. I do not think we are asking too much when we suggest that a policy of this type be laid down. It might have to be a broad, long term policy at this stage but there is certainly need for a program which we can see and understand.
There is one further aspect of oil development which I should like to see discussed in the house. I am thinking about Canada's continental shelf areas-there is one off the west coast of British Columbia, there is one off the east coast and another in the Arctic region which may prove to be one of the largest oil reserves in the entire world.
We have all heard of the major oil discoveries in Alaska and I believe there is no doubt that these resources extend into the Arctic waters which we in Canada have always claimed as our own. In this respect, I feel it is high time the government made a clear pronouncement as to the jurisdiction which we in Canada expect to exercise in this area, because these reserves could be a terrific asset to our nation in years to come. It is not many years ago that areas in the Arctic were looked upon as nothing more than vast frozen wastes to be ignored by people of all nations. Other countries have since found that there are vast stores of riches in these areas.
DEBATES	7563
Oil and Gas Production and Conservation We in Canada must be mindful of this situation and I am certain the government is aware of the necessity of staking out a real claim, one which cannot be disputed, as far as our Arctic regions are concerned.
To get back to the subject of the continental shelf, I should like to hear from the minister a clear indication of the government's intention with regard to these areas. According to reports I have read there is a great potential on the Atlantic side of Canada. If oil were to be discovered there in substantial amounts, there is no doubt it would go a long way to assisting an area which is greatly in need of assistance; the per capita income of the inhabitants could be greatly increased and a long step taken toward the reduction of regional disparity. Exploration programs could well be undertaken, perhaps with assistance from the federal government working very closely with the provinces concerned, in which case something might well come out of it.
I shall not spend more time on the subject now. I presume there are other hon. members who wish to speak on this bill. When it goes to the committee some amendments may be moved to the various clauses.
Before I sit down, I would again press the minister to give the house some clear cut information as to the government's oil and gas conservation program in much more detail than is outlined in the bill before us. He should give Canadians a much better indication of the course which the government proposes to take. I, personally, would welcome an assurance that all these potential oil resources in the north with which the bill is concerned are to be retained as far as possible by Canadians in the interests of Canada. I leave this thought with the minister, assuring him that this feeling is very widespread in this country. I trust the policies and programs evolved by his department will lead in this direction.

speakeroldname: Mr. R. J. Orange (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: OIL AND GAS PRODUCTION AND CONSERVATION
subtopic: MEASURE ESTABLISHING OIL AND GAS COMMITTEE, AND REGULATING POWERS OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this bill has been given to us at a most appropriate moment in our history of resource development in the north.
Like many other members in this chamber I returned to my constituency during the past ten days. One of the areas in which I spent a considerable time was the Mackenzie Delta which is under fairly extensive exploration by the oil companies. It is not difficult to sense the enthusiasm, the excitement which
April 15, 1969
7564	COMMONS
Oil and Gas Production and Conservation exists in this far north western part of our country, an excitement generated by the activities of the companies involved in the search for oil. I hope the companies concerned meet with a great deal of success. At a place called Tatoonik and another called Tuk-toyaktuk we happened to fly over oil drilling rigs drilling right on the Arctic coast. We listened to the rumours. We followed accounts from the oil companies which appeared in the newspapers. We see that what is happening at the moment is only, if I may use the term, a drop in the bucket in terms of the kind of activity that will take place in the search for oil in northern Canada during the next 3, 5, 10 or 20 years.
[DOT] (9:40 p.ra.)
Both this afternoon and this evening we have listened to hon. members of this house talk of the implications, the complications and the ramifications of oil development in northern Canada. I think that all of us as Canadians are anxious to see a resource development in northern Canada that will benefit not only the north but improve the economic wellbeing of us all.
I do not want to repeat the arguments that have been made or the discussion that has taken place, but there are a couple of areas upon which I should like to touch. With regard to some things that may and hopefully will occur in the months and years to come, neither the companies involved in this exploration nor the governments who will be responsible for the production and conservation of oil and gas should forget those people who live in the particular areas concerned.
At the moment some of the major exploration companies across the country are doing a reasonable job in the encouragement of employment among people who were born, raised and educated in northern Canada. Unfortunately, other companies are not doing as well as they should in this regard. I should like to think that about half of the seismic crews, which I am told consist of approximately 28 people, should be recruited from people living in the north, provided there is some consultation with and engagement of the government, particularly the vocational training people in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Canada Manpower Service. If this were the case, then perhaps not this year but in one, two or three years many of our young people in the north-and the older people as well provided they are interested and are properly
IMr. Orange.]

trained-can truly participate in this exciting venture.
I also think that some of the companies involved in this exploration should examine their wage scales. In terms of gross wages the remuneration is not really that bad; in terms of hourly pay for working in the bush the wage amounts to about $1.50 per hour for perhaps 350 hours a month, not including overtime. To their credit the companies have made no attempt to circumvent the present wage legislation that has been passed by the territorial government.
The second point here at which I believe we, as Canadians and myself as a northerner, have to look is that we do not want to see the north exploited and become a gravel pit for the use of industries south of the 60th parallel. In other words, we in the north want our fair share of the activity. I recognize that it may be difficult to develop industries that require power derived from our oil and gas resources, but I also recognize there are ways and means of ensuring growth beyond the mere taking of products out of the ground, pumping them through a pipe line and shipping them to places in southern Canada and the United States.
I think this is one area that the minister and his department, having taken upon themselves the responsibility of conservation, and combined with their other responsibility for northern development, must look upon as a primary function. I should like to think that in the course of the discussions in the committee the suggestion will be made, preferably by the minister, that there are ways and means of ensuring that some of the potential benefits to be derived from this area will remain in northern Canada. I am not saying that selfishly; I am saying it because I believe that if we are to be a nation of three dimensions we must have economic development and growth not just along the narrow band north of the United States border.
If we are successful in this regard I think we can look to immediate benefits. The growth and construction of gas and oil lines will have an impact upon the community and will open up communications and transportation routes in areas in the north. However, I believe we must look far beyond this.
During the course of speeches made this afternoon and evening members have asked: Tell us now what is happening with Panarctic. Can we get some clear cut information? How many acres are under the control of this
April 15, 1969

company? I think that most of this information has been made public. I believe that the Panarctic venture on the part of government and industry is an exciting one and one in which the government has declared there are two alternatives, either to make an outright grant under present guidelines or to participate.
A great deal of activity is taking place in the Arctic islands in Panarctic's search. Even if this search is not successful, I think it will produce most important and valuable information regarding what does exist in this part of Canada. I think it has also informed Canadians that this is their land. There has been a lot of discussion regarding sovereignty and this area, and I think that once again governmental activity has established Canadian sovereignty over the Arctic islands as a result of the Panarctic oil program.
Again, I should like to impress upon the minister that in the process of developing a policy in regard to the use of oil and gas in northern Canada we should not forget for one moment the Indian, Eskimo, Metis and white people of the north. They, too, must participate, in some real and viable fashion, in what is potentially an opportunity for great economic growth.
I should also like to re-emphasize to the minister that the north must not become a gravel pit. If resources are there to be developed, then as a result of such development some benefit must accrue in terms of growth and economic development to northern Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. James Richardson (for the Minister of Transport) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENTS DEFINING "AIR CUSHION VEHICLE" AND CLARIFYING OTHER PROVISIONS
speechtext:
that Bill S-23, to amend the Canada Shipping Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill S-23 contains a variety of amendments to the Canada Shipping Act which is, as hon. members know, one of the lengthiest of our statutes. Hon. members will recall that only recently the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) announced plans for a complete revision of
Canada Shipping Act
the Canada Shipping Act. The amendments now before us are ones that cannot wait for this major revision.
The bill contains our first legislative provisions concerning the new type of conveyance called an air cushion vehicle. This type of vehicle of course is also referred to as a hovercraft. Until now these vehicles have been subject to regulations under the Aeronautics Act; but, as air cushion vehicles are really surface vehicles the Aeronautics Act is not the appropriate act under which to regulate them. Hon. members will recall that an amendment to the Aeronautics Act received royal assent last month. This amendment, when it is proclaimed, will remove air cushion vehicles from the definition of aircraft and they will no longer be subject to the Aeronautics Act.
I should like to make it clear that we do not intend air cushion vehicles to be regarded as ships but only that they shall be subject to some of the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act in the same manner as ships are when they are being operated over the surface of the water. The provisions we are proposing in this regard must be considered as an interim measure only. There seems to be no doubt that ultimately we will need special legislation for air cushion vehicles, but I believe this would be premature at this time. It will be premature until we know much more about these new craft and how they are likely to develop.
There is also provision in Bill S-23 to allow landed immigrants to hold certificates as masters, mates and engineers on ships, a privilege now restricted to British subjects. Provision is also made in this bill to permit regulations to be passed requiring ships of 9 tons gross tonnage and over to be subject to inspection. The present lower limit is 15 tons, gross tonnage.
In order to complement the provisions of the Canada Labour (Safety) Code there is provision for making regulations on the subject of accident prevention aboard ship and a provision respecting the reporting of accidents that occur on ships. Another clause requires the reporting of other accidents, such as collisions or groundings of ships in our waters. Heretofore only accidents to British ships were required to be reported.
There is a provision for regulations to be made on the subject of pollution of our waters by garbage, sewage and other matters from ships and there is a provision that will allow any wrecked vessel to be removed if it

April 15, 1969
Canada Shipping Act
is causing pollution or likely to do so. Provision is also made for regulations to be made requiring all vessels in our waters to be fitted with radio installations. This has been found necessary for traffic control purposes.
In order to remove some doubts as to the validity of some of our by-laws and procedures in the administration of pilotage, there is a provision stating that all existing by-laws are valid.
In order that we may give effect to the provisions of the International Convention on Load Lines, 1966, there are amendments to bring the provisions of the act into line with that convention.
Finally, there are a number of miscellaneous items such as the repeal of certain archaic sections relating to seamen and provisions giving some uniformity to the sections relating to offences and penalties. POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT-VANCOUVER- PERMANENT EMPLOYEES TO REPLACE THOSE HAVING CASUAL STATUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been rather persistent in bringing up this matter of casual employees in the post office. I regret to keep a busy minister up late so many nights. I realize that the problem of casual employees in the post office is not new. The casuals were employed there long before the minister took over the portfolio. The minister himself has outlined a number of reasons for having casual employees, reasons which are also outlined in the post office personnel manual. There is mention of the Christmas rush, vacations, sick leave and end of month provisions, and I do not think anyone quarrels with those.
I realize also that in the change-over period brought on by implementing the five day week and by introducing other technological, changes about 2,000 people who have been permanently employed in the post office must be placed in new positions. This takes some time. What bothers me, that bothers many postal workers and many other people of this country, is the preponderance of casual employees in the post office at the present time. To me, this looks like a deliberate attempt to lower the total wage cost. The department is attempting to employ casuals on a more or less full time basis and save money. If that is not contrary to the letter of the act, it certainly is contrary to its spirit and contrary to what is contained in the postal service personnel manual.
I checked some figures and as of two weeks ago these are some of the figures relating to the major post offices across Canada. I will give total figures, Mr. Speaker. In Vancouver, British Columbia, there are 105 casual employees. In St. John's, Newfoundland, there are ten; in Saint John, New Brunswick, there are eight; in Montreal 245; in Moncton, 21; and Trois-Rivieres, where some casual employees are working a 40 hour week now to fill vacancies, there is a total of nine.
The people at the Regina post office refused to divulge the number of casual employees there, but it is presumed that there are quite a number there. Winnipeg has 90; Hamilton
April 15, 1969
95; Quebec a total of 65 in various sections, not all on extended sick leave; Halifax 22; Sherbrooke, Quebec, none; North Bay, 14; Edmonton, 58; London, 60; Windsor, I was unable to get the figures except for the total number of hours and Scarborough, 48. The Postmaster in Saskatoon said he did not have authority to divulge such information. In New Westminster, the total is 22 and in Sudbury, 20.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
This is quite a number. Many people, especially those employed or attempting to be employed by the Post Office, are extremely concerned about this. I obtained this information as a result of a telegram from the Vancouver postal workers which reads in part:
There are over one hundred casuals employed and one hundred applicants have successfully qualified for positions.
I previously confirmed the number of casuals employed in Vancouver.
According to information which I have received, 26 full time positions have been promised in the Ottawa post office, but so far none have been confirmed. I believe I am correct in saying that the agreement reached on the five-day week in February contemplated a 60-day freeze on permanent positions so that present employees' jobs might be protected during the reorganization period. It is now three days from the expiry of the deadline and I hope the minister will tell the house what chance there is of relieving this rather discouraging casual picture across Canada which I have outlined before the expiry date.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, in answer to the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) on May 17, as recorded at page 6685 of Hansard, the minister said in part:
This afternoon the officers of the department will be discussing the letter with me, and they will also be discussing with the officers of the Ottawa Post Office Unions the reasons which caused them to send such a letter and the problem concerning the use of casuals.
He later goes on to say:
However, this is a problem that we are willing to discuss fully with them.
What I would like to learn is whether the minister or his officials have met and discussed this casual situation with the Ottawa Post Office unions. If not, when can we expect him to do so?

speakeroldname: Hon. Eric W. Kierans (Minister of Communications):
maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT-VANCOUVER- PERMANENT EMPLOYEES TO REPLACE THOSE HAVING CASUAL STATUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion has given all the reasons why there was an increase in the number of casuals during the last several months. Because of the changeover to a five day week and because of our assurance that no permanent employees would lose their jobs-they were guaranteed security-after the middle of October we did not engage any new personnel. Obviously, the work of the Post Office has to keep on going, We employed casuals or part-timers while we were keeping these jobs open.
I quarrel with a report in the Globe and Mail which said that the Post Office overtime has been on the rise. The report refers to our use of casuals. The fact is after the conversion to a five-day week overtime has decreased in the Post Office and the number of casuals is going down continuously. We are discussing this with the union. We are as concerned about the problem as they are.
I may say in respect of the Ottawa post office that the union spokesman who made the charge of nepotism against the post office was, let us say, embarrassed by a questioner on a television program who said it was his understanding that the charge of nepotism could be equally divided between those who were officers in the post office in Ottawa and those who were union members. This turned out to be true. Of something like a little over 100 casuals, 35 could be said to have obtained their jobs because of knowing people inside the post office. On the other hand, about half of them attained their positions because they knew a member of the union. We are plagued with this problem in the post office. We are attempting to work it out with the union. We have an abnormally high sick leave which averages three per cent to four per cent above that in the Civil Service as a whole. There really is no reason for it. We are investigating this and I feel we will work out a solution with the unions. It really is a question of morale.
I want to deny emphatically the implied charge that we are using casuals in an attempt to reduce our costs or the average wage paid in the post office. This is completely untrue. We use casuals because of the nature of the work in the post office. The loads occur at different times. We do not use them for any other reason.
